answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
3Degrees supports consequential accounting as a valuable tool for assessing the real‑world emissions impacts of corporate actions. This approach shifts focus from inventory metrics to actual emission reductions, enabling companies to identify and disclose interventions that produce tangible decarbonization outcomes. However, realizing this potential requires more than revised calculation methods. Without clarity on how reporters would apply these methods—or how results would connect to existing corporate inventories—it is difficult to evaluate their implications or provide meaningful feedback.

Adopting standard approaches always involves trade-offs, where the benefits provided by the standardized approach are weighed against the cost, level-of-effort, constraints, practice changes, data availability, and other factors that implementing the standard would require. With this in mind, examining an accounting method in isolation with no commentary on its purpose or use, leaves us stymied as to how to evaluate these tradeoffs. Furthermore, a consultation structured in this way risks failing to attract appropriate stakeholder attention such that potentially important points of view are never heard.

As such, 3Degrees is concerned that the GHGP proposed Consequential Accounting Methods for Electricity-Sector Emissions lacks sufficient guidance and clarity regarding its intended purpose for a productive consultation.

Mature consequential accounting methods for the electricity sector already exist, including those within the GHG Protocol. It is unclear what additional value a new method adds or how it fits within current reporting frameworks. Given ISO’s 2024 reaffirmation of ISO 14064‑2:2019 as a still-current standard for project accounting—and ongoing ISO/GHGP harmonization—introducing a new GHGP method now seems unnecessary and poorly timed.

Third, while the issue of “mutual exclusivity” is not addressed in the proposed Consequential Accounting Methods for Electricity-sector Emissions, we understand the topic is still being considered within the Actions and Market Instruments discussions. As such, we here posit that the contractual ledger and the impact ledger do not need to be mutually exclusive.
Many companies seek to understand the impact of their actions in both attributional and consequential terms, as the two expressions convey distinct but critical information about intervention impacts. Companies should be able to claim and report both kinds of information to their customers and stakeholders, provided it is clear that the two ledgers are not additive.

By using the consequential Scope 2 methods, companies can identify where to pursue PPAs or source RECs from specific suppliers to maximize impact and should be able to quantify and disclose those benefits. At the same time, they should retain the ability to report a full market‑based inventory using allocational accounting. The two approaches provide distinct yet complementary insights into real‑world impact and overall GHG performance. Limiting reporting to one ledger would restrict transparency and flexibility.

Lastly, 3Degrees is concerned about the sequence of decisions leading up to this consultation, as the materials in the GHGP’s Standards Development and Governance Repository appear misaligned with this first public consultation, and there has been insufficient transparency and accountability regarding how and why this shift occurred. Per GHGP’s strengthened governance model, trust and transparency are foundational because the standards only function effectively when market actors and regulators can see that the rules are fair, stable, and applied consistently across all users. We recommend that GHGP clearly explain how and why the content of this consultation diverges from the direction previously discussed in the Scope 2 TWG and the consequential accounting subgroup, including the rationale for any substantive changes.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The Section 6 proposal language is, frankly, confusing so we are uncertain how best to comment and simply cannot affirm that the proposal is appropriate. Here are central points of our confusion:

The text in 6.1 states that the TWG proposal is intended to “capture the emissions impacts of electricity projects” while the headline statement in 6.0 states the proposal is intended to “quantify consequential emissions impacts from electricity procurement.” Further, the formula itself uses the variable “MWh procured.”

Procurement assessment and new-built project assessment are different aims. Not every procurement involves a new project, not every procurement is a low-carbon initiative, not every procurement is specific to the time and place of specific generation resources. As worded, the formula could be interpreted as attempting to sum up the emissions associated with all electricity purchased by a reporter in the reporting year. This interpretation aligns with the language “emission impacts from electricity procurement.”

We suspect however that the TWG’s intention is to provide a formula representing the reporting-year benefits of low-carbon MWhs procured and claimed in a company’s market-based Scope 2 inventory. In this case, the formula provides an “avoided emissions” calculation pertaining to these procured MWh. We note that the word “impact” can have either positive or negative connotations, so our interpretation is uncertain. As to scope, the formula’s intended use might be limited to certain kinds of procurements (Whole projects? New projects (new when?) Do tariffs count? etc. We note the phrase “electricity project generation” in the middle of page 8 and in the text of Question 19, but we are not clear on the specifics here.

Without a clearer understanding of the TWG’s intention and, as noted in our response to Question 18, without an idea of the proposed use of these calculations, we are unable to provide tuned commentary and cannot affirm the formula’s appropriateness.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: The types of secondary effects we’d recommend considering would depend on the purpose of the calculation method. That said, we’d encourage the GHGP to consider including recurring upstream secondary effects. These recurring effects could be substantial in some instances, particularly for renewable energy projects that displace fossil-generated electricity because of ongoing upstream emissions from fuel extraction, processing, transport, and methane leakage associated with fossil-generated electricity. In the first year, the effects may appear modest once you include the emissions from manufacturing renewable energy assets (e.g., solar panels), but in subsequent years, as the renewable project continues to avoid fuel‑cycle emissions, avoided emissions are significant. Ignoring this dynamic, or failing to recognize it explicitly for solar and other renewables, leads to an incomplete and potentially misleading picture of their true emissions benefits. Some additional relevant secondary effects GHGP could consider include the year‑by‑year changes in project economics as renewable penetration increases, which in turn create incentives to add storage to both existing and new projects.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Emissions impacts should be calculated and reported each reporting year, with ex post data. Annual reporting allows year-specific generation and grid emissions data to be reflected in results and aligns with annual corporate inventory cycles. Reporting a project’s lifetime impacts at the outset would require assumptions about lifetime generation and grid conditions, which may diverge from measured generation and grid emissions data in later years.

Note that without an understanding of the purpose and use of these calculations, we cannot be certain that our answer here is firm. For example, estimating emission benefits to be derived from forward-looking, long-term procurement contracts is a common feature of many buyer decision-making processes. For this purpose, only a forward-looking, whole-life estimate is appropriate.

For what it’s worth, it is not obvious what stakeholder actions will be influenced by an annual procurement impact metric that sits alongside inventory metrics. Especially with a scope 2 market-based proposal that severely narrows the geographic range of qualifying electricity procurements - hence precluding reporters from pursuing high-emissions-impact options if their load is in a clean-grid location - it is just not clear what decision-useful information the metric will convey.

answers.label: Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
3Degrees does not support the inclusion of any additionality standard in the consequential accounting guidance. This is for programmatic reasons, electricity system reasons, and to maintain the integrity and transparency of the accounted emissions.

Programmatic role:
The GHGP should offer guidance similar to ISO 14064‑2, where they require the project to define and justify a baseline scenario representing what would reasonably have happened without the project and to quantify the emissions impact relative to that baseline, without passing judgment on the project’s key causal factors. This is because there are many legitimate ways to apply project accounting and the resulting emission calculations, not all of which require proof of causation.

Instead, the standard should leave additionality questions to programs and users to layer in where and when appropriate to their purposes.

Electricity System:
In most of the world, electricity project development is enabled by a large ecosystem of stakeholders, often competing for development opportunities. While corporate offtakers can play an important role in bringing new projects to fruition, it is a dynamic market and it now stretches credibility to assert that any one company’s particular action was causal; another buyer would be right behind, and in any case the developments are economically advantageous for their developers, financiers, and other participants. It is for this (and other) reasons that carbon credit program authorities stopped validating new renewable energy-based carbon projects in developed countries, several years ago.

Integrity and transparency

Even if programmatic and electricity system factors were not at play, we would not recommend additionality tests in this standard. Additionality tests purport to confirm or prove the level-of-importance a specific actor plays in a complex transaction involving many parties. Even when prescriptive, they are prone to error and controversy.

Rather than attempting to prescribe the ideal additionality test, we believe it is more credible and transparent to avoid them altogether, and make clear that the emissions impact calculations represent the impact of the project without asserting any causal relationship between the reporter and the project’s realization. In this way, stakeholders can decide whether to embrace the emission benefits as important and relevant to the reporter’s performance, or not. As they see fit.
